title: Jury hears details of police shooting
article: A Midland man - suffering from mental illness and claiming to hear voices - was brandishing two knives when shot by a Midland police officer, a coroner's inquest heard Monday.
During her opening remarks, coroner's counsel Allison MacPherson outlined the circumstances leading up to the shooting of 38-year-old Douglas Heagle at his Scott Street residence on Feb. 3, 2009.

"He had a knife in each hand and continued to advance towards Const. (Mike) Sibley," MacPherson told the five-member jury. "Const. Sibley drew his service revolver and struck Douglas Heagle in the abdomen."

The inquest, which is expected to last five days, will examine the circumstances surrounding Heagle's death. After all evidence and witnesses have been heard, the jury is empowered to make recommendations aimed at preventing similar deaths.
An audio recording played for the jury outlined just how quickly events transpired after Heagle's mother Betty called 911 shortly before 5 p.m.
Four officers eventually arrived at the scene. Three entered the home and were confronted by Heagle, who the jury heard was clutching several large kitchen knives.

The inquest heard that Heagle eventually made his way outside, ignoring police orders to drop the knives and advancing toward an officer, who was backed up against a snowbank. At that point, Sibley fired his gun one time, striking Heagle.
A short while later, another officer can be heard saying on the recording: "Mike had to shoot somebody. He came out with two knives."
Police are subsequently heard on the tape organizing who will attend each specific scene, including Georgian Bay General Hospital, where Heagle was taken and pronounced dead at 5:59 p.m.

Despite the fact Heagle had succumbed to his injuries, his mother still wasn't aware her son had been shot and had died when she was interviewed by Special Investigations Unit (SIU) officers at a neighbour's home just after 8 p.m. It is not clear when she finally learned her son was dead.
Betty Heagle was unable to attend the inquest due to poor health, so the SIU interview was played for jurors.
During the nearly 30-minute interview, Betty Heagle said she tried to call 911 several times, but her son, who she described as being out of control, kept hanging up the phone.
"He started smashing pictures with his hands and the TV," she recounted. "Doug is not normally a bad person, but he does hear voices. It's been a long haul."

Betty Heagle, who is now in her early 70s, said her son didn't drink or take drugs except for those prescribed for his "psychiatric problems." Besides hearing voices, she said, he was afraid to leave the house and was prone to seizures.
"I kept saying to him, he needs to move around and get outside, but he just sits there," Heagle told SIU investigators, who asked her on the tape if she knows what has happened to her son.
"No, I don't," she replied. "But I don't want a charge laid against him."
Betty Heagle said she didn't hear any gunshots and only saw her son on the ground at the side of their home surrounded by officers.
"I think they acted appropriately," she said. "I think they did their job."

Douglas Heagle was born to First Nations parents in Flin Flon, Man. Suffering from fetal-alcohol syndrome, he was adopted by Betty Heagle at the age of six weeks. According to MacPherson, he had a Grade 10 education and an intelligence quotient (IQ) of about 80.

The Heagle family moved to Midland from Newmarket and had lived on Scott Street for about eight years prior to the incident. At the time of his death, Heagle weighed 169 pounds and stood five feet six inches.

Pathologist Dr. Nihad Ali-Ridha conducted a post-mortem in Toronto two days after the shooting. He testified Heagle died from major blood loss caused by a single gunshot wound that perforated several vital organs, including his kidney, liver and stomach.
"The bullet didn't exit the body because it mushroomed out," Ali-Ridha told the jury. "It was a hollow-point projectile."

John Weiler is a use-of-force instructor at the Ontario Police College. He said in most cases, edged weapons - which run the gamut from knives to screwdrivers to razor blades affixed to credit cards - pose a greater danger than firearms.

"They're extremely dangerous and have incredible potential to maim or kill," said Weiler, who worked as a policeman for 11 years in Peel Region. "Even from 20 feet away, you're not safe from an edged weapon."
Weiler said officers are trained to shoot above the torso since hitting an appendage can be difficult when a suspect is agitated or moving.
"By shooting at an appendage, you're aiming at a small area," he said. "You could miss or hit someone else."
The SIU issued a report on March 27, 2009, that concluded no reasonable grounds existed to believe Sibley committed a crime in shooting the knife-wielding man.
On Monday, presiding coroner Dr. David Eden told jurors they will play a critical role by carefully assessing all evidence and witness statements.
"Your findings don't have to be unanimous, only a majority finding," Eden said. "You must consider all evidence and keep an open mind."
